In the mathematical theory of [[probability]], a '''generalized renewal process (GRP) ''' or '''G-renewal process''' is a stochastic point process used to model failure/repair behavior of repairable systems in [[reliability engineering]]. [[Poisson point process]] is a particular case of GRP.

== Probabilistic model ==
=== Virtual age ===
The G-renewal process is introduced by [[Masaaki Kijima|Kijima]] and Sumita through the notion of the ''virtual age''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kijima |first1=Masaaki|last2=Sumita|first2=Ushio |title=A Useful Generalization of Renewal Theory: Counting Processes Governed by Non-Negative Markovian Increments |journal=Journal of Applied Probability |year=1986 |volume=23 |issue=1 |pages=71–88 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3214117 |publisher=Applied Probability Trust|doi=10.2307/3214117 |jstor=3214117 |s2cid=222275620 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> 
:<math>y_i = q t_i </math>
::where:
:: <math> t_i </math> and <math> y_i </math> is real and virtual age (respectively) of the system at/after the ''i''{{sup|th}} repair,
:: <math> q </math> is the ''restoration factor'' (a.k.a., repair effectiveness factor),
::::<math> q=0 </math>, represents the condition of a perfect repair, where the system age is reset to zero after the repair. This condition corresponds to the ''Ordinary Renewal Process''.
::::<math> q=1 </math>, represents the condition of a minimal repair, where the system condition after the repair remains the same as right before the repair. This condition corresponds to the ''Non-Homogeneous Poisson Process''.
::::<math> 0<q<1 </math>, represents the condition of a general repair, where the system condition is between perfect repair and minimal repair. This condition corresponds to the ''Generalized Renewal Process''.
Kaminskiy and Krivtsov <ref name="foo">{{cite book |last1= Kaminskiy |first1= M.P.|last2= Krivtsov|first2= V.V.|date= 1998|chapter= A Monte Carlo approach to repairable system reliability analysis|title= Probabilistic Safety Assessment and Management|location= London|url = http://www.bookfinder4u.com/IsbnSearch.aspx?isbn=3540762620&mode=direct| publisher= Springer–Verlag|pages= 1063–1068}}</ref> extended the [[Masaaki Kijima|Kijima]] models by allowing ''q''&nbsp;>&nbsp;1, so that the repair damages (ages) the system to a higher degree than it was just before the respective failure.

===G-renewal equation===
Mathematically, the G-renewal process is quantified through the solution of the G-renewal equation:
:<math>W(t) = \int_0^t(  g(\tau \mid 0) + \int_0^\tau w(x) \cdot (g(\tau - x \mid x) \,dx  )\,d\tau </math>
:where,
::<math>g(\tau \mid x) = \frac{(t+qx,\theta)}{1-F(qx,\theta)}</math>   <math> t,x \geq 0 </math>
::<math> w(x) = \frac{dW(x)}{dx} </math>   
:: ''f''(''t'') is the [[Probability density function|probability density function (PDF)]] of the underlying failure time distribution,
:: ''F''(''t'') is the [[cumulative distribution function]] (CDF) of the underlying failure time distribution,
:: ''q'' is the restoration factor,
:: <math> {\theta} </math> is the vector of parameters of the underlying failure-time distribution.
A [[Closed-form expression|closed-form solution]] to the G-renewal equation is not possible. Also, numerical approximations are difficult to obtain due to the recurrent infinite series. A [[Monte Carlo method|Monte Carlo]] based approach to solving the G-renewal equation was developed by Kaminiskiy and Krivtsov.<ref name="foo" /><ref>{{cite thesis |type=PhD |last=Krivtsov |first=V. V. |date=2000 |title=Modeling and estimation of the generalized renewal process in repairable system reliability analysis |url=https://catalog.umd.edu/F/?func=find-b&local%5Fbase=cp&find%5Fcode=035&request=ocm47871209&pds%5Fhandle=GUEST&pds%5Fhandle=GUEST&pds%5Fhandle=GUEST&pds_handle=GUEST |publisher=University of Maryland, College Park, ISBN/ISSN: 0599725877}}</ref>

== Statistical estimation == 
The G–renewal process gained its practical popularity in [[reliability engineering]] only after methods for estimating its parameters had become available.

=== Monte Carlo approach ===
The [[Non-linear least squares|nonlinear LSQ estimation]] of the G–renewal process was first offered by Kaminskiy & Krivtsov.<ref name="foo" /> A random inter-arrival time from a parameterized G-Renewal process is given by:
:<math>X_i = F^{-1} (1-U_i[1- F(qS_{i-1})]) - qS_{i-1} </math>
: where,
:: <math> S_{i-1} </math> is the cumulative real age before the i{{sup|th}} inter-arrival,
:: <math> U_i </math> is a uniformly distributed [[random variable]],
:: <math> F </math> is the [[Cumulative distribution function|CDF]] of the underlying failure-time distribution.
The Monte Carlo solution was subsequently improved<ref>{{cite book |last= Yevkin |first= A.|editor-first1= Christophe|editor-first2= Antoine|editor-first3= Carlos|editor-last1= Berenguer|editor-last2= Grall|editor-last3= Guedes Soares|date= 2011|chapter= Monte Carlo Approach for Evaluation of Availability and Failure Intensity under G–Renewal Process Model|title= Advances in Safety, Reliability and Risk Management|location= London|url = https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/mono/10.1201/b11939/advances-safety-reliability-risk-management-christophe-berenguer-antoine-grall-carlos-guedes-soares| publisher= CRC Press|pages= 1015–1020|doi= 10.1201/b11939|isbn= 9780429217265}}</ref> and implemented as a web resource.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.soft4structures.com/WeibullGRP/JSPageGRP.jsp|title= G-Renewal Process Calculator|last= Yevkin |first= A.|access-date= May 13, 2021}}</ref>

=== Maximum likelihood approach ===
The [[Maximum likelihood estimation|maximum likelihood]] procedures were subsequently discussed by Yañez, et al.,<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Yañez |first1= M. |last2= Joglar |first2= F.|last3= Modarres |first3= M.|date= August 2002|title= Generalized renewal process for analysis of repairable systems with limited failure experience |url= https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0951832002000443|journal= Reliability Engineering & System Safety |volume=  77|issue= 2|pages= 167–180|doi= 10.1016/S0951-8320(02)00044-3 |url-access= subscription}}</ref> and Mettas & Zhao.<ref>{{cite conference |url= https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/1408358|title= Modeling and analysis of repairable systems with general repair
|last1= Mettas|first1= A.|last2= Zhao|first2= W.|date= 24 January 2005|location= Alexandria, VA
|conference= Annual Reliability and Maintainability Symposium 2005}}</ref> The estimation of the G–renewal restoration factor was addressed in detail by Kahle & Love.<ref>{{cite book |last1= Kahle |first1= W. |last2= Love|first2= C. |title= Mathematical and Statistical Methods in Reliability |chapter= Modeling the Influence of Maintenance Actions |series= Series on Quality, Reliability and Engineering Statistics |date= 2003|url= https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/9789812795250_0025 |volume= 7 |pages= 387–399|doi= 10.1142/9789812795250_0025 |isbn= 978-981-238-321-1 |url-access= subscription }}</ref>

=== Regularization method in estimating GRP parameters ===
The estimation of G–renewal process parameters is an ill–posed [[inverse problem]], and therefore, the solution may not be unique and is sensitive to the input data. Krivtsov & Yevkin<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Krivtsov|first1= V.V. |last2= Yevkin|first2= O.|date= July 2013|title= Estimation of G-renewal process parameters as an ill-posed inverse problem |url= https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0951832013000409|journal= Reliability Engineering & System Safety |volume=  115|pages= 10–18|doi= 10.1016/j.ress.2013.02.005 |url-access= subscription}}</ref><ref>{{cite conference |url= https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7889707|title= Regularization techniques for recurrent failure prediction under Kijima models|last1= Krivtsov|first1= Vasiliy|last2= Yevkin|first2= Alex|date= 2017|location= Orlando, FL|conference= Annual Reliability and Maintainability Symposium 2017}}</ref> suggested first to estimate the underlying distribution parameters using the time to first failures only. Then, the obtained parameters are used as the initial values for the second step, whereat all model parameters (including the restoration factor(s)) are estimated simultaneously. This approach allows, on the one hand, to avoid irrelevant solutions (wrong local maximums or minimums of the objective function) and on the other hand, to improve computational speed, as the number of iterations significantly depends on the selected initial values.

== Limitations ==

One limitation of the Generalized Renewal Process is that it cannot account for "better-than-new" repair. <ref>{{cite arXiv |last1= Kaminskiy|first1= M.P. |last2= Krivtsov|first2= V.V.|date= June 2010|title= G1-Renewal Process as Repairable System Model |class= stat.ME |eprint= 1006.3718 }}</ref> The [[G1-renewal process]] has been developed which applies the restoration factor to the life parameter of a location-scale distribution to be able to account for "better-than-new" repair in addition to other repair types.
